READING

**What Local Voice demands and where each course lands**

The three qualifying conditions are: fourteen hours a week of originated speech, commissioned production no more than half of that originated total, and thirty registered contributors. The assessment date is 2027-02-28. Missing it triggers a single re-sit on 2027-08-31, after which payment begins only in the month of clearance while the four-year clock still starts 2027-04-01.

---

**ELSWICK: does it qualify?**

Cost: 6 hours × 52 weeks × £65 = £20,280 a year. Within the £22,000 board cap. ✓

Hours: 9 current + 6 Halverston = 15 hours a week. One hour clear of the mark. ✓

Commissioned cap: 6 commissioned hours out of 15 total = 40 %. The ceiling is 50 %. Comfortably under. ✓

Contributors: no movement. Register stays at 34. Above the 30 minimum. ✓

February 2027 compliance: delivered on a signed contract. Certainty, not a projection.

Rate risk: Halverston's rate is held at £65 only to 2026-12-31. The rolling twelve-month contract starting 2026-10-05 runs through 2027-10-04. The February assessment falls inside that first term, so the locked rate covers the qualifying period. After October 2027, renegotiation will happen. At £65 the cost is £20,280; the board cap of £22,000 would be breached if the rate rose above roughly £70.50. That is a future risk, not an immediate one.

Long-term margin under Local Voice: £96,000 − £58,000 − £20,280 = **£17,720 a year**, but only if Halverston hours are maintained permanently, because none of this content sits on the station's roster.

Register trend: the register is falling, 41 in 2024, 34 now, roughly three to four losses a year. Under ELSWICK there is no dedicated effort to reverse that. By February 2027 the number is likely around 32, still above 30. In subsequent years it could approach the threshold with nothing arresting the slide.

---

**CRANMOOR: does it qualify?**

Cost: £21,000 a year with on-costs. Within the board cap. ✓

Hours: the station currently carries 9 hours from the volunteer roster. The target is 14, so 5 additional hours a week need to come from new contributors. The problem itself states that reaching 14 hours requires approximately 15 new contributors. These are not commissioned and carry no cap exposure.

The operational question is whether 15 new active contributors can be recruited and scheduled in the window between 2026-10-01 and 2027-02-28: roughly five months.

Historical rate: 9 contributors added across the whole of 2025, with no coordinator. That is 0.75 a month. To land 15 in five months requires 3 a month — four times the established rate. A half-time coordinator dedicated to recruitment and the register would accelerate things, but a fourfold acceleration in five months is a large ask. If the coordinator doubles the rate to 1.5 a month, the station recruits about 7 or 8 new contributors and adds perhaps 2 to 3 hours a week, reaching 11 to 12 hours. That is short. Reaching 14 hours demands that the coordinator sustains something close to the full fourfold improvement from day one, with no ramp-up period, and that each new recruit actually contributes scheduled programming hours and not just joins the register.

**If CRANMOOR misses February 2027:**

The current grant expires 2027-03-31. The re-sit is 2027-08-31. Payment, if cleared, begins September 2027. The gap is April through August — five months with no grant income.

Monthly burn (fixed costs plus coordinator salary): (£58,000 + £21,000) ÷ 12 = £6,583.
Five-month reserve draw: approximately £32,900.
Reserve position after: approximately £29,100 — the station survives, but half the reserve is gone.
Lost Local Voice income (five months at £96,000 a year): approximately £40,000.
Combined financial impact of failure: roughly £73,000, against a £62,000 reserve.

That combination — reserve depleted to roughly half and a substantial permanent loss of grant — is a severe outcome, and the reserve never fully recovers under normal running margins.

Long-term margin under Local Voice if CRANMOOR succeeds: £96,000 − £58,000 − £21,000 = **£17,000 a year**, with content owned, no annual purchase, and the register actively managed.

---

**Comparing the two**

| | ELSWICK | CRANMOOR |
|---|---|---|
| February 2027 compliance | Contractually certain | Requires 4× historical recruitment rate in 5 months |
| Annual margin under Local Voice | £17,720 | £17,000 |
| Content ownership | None — bought every year | Permanent |
| Register trend | Unaddressed | Actively managed |
| Risk of grant gap | None | Material (≈£73k combined impact) |

The annual margin difference is £720. That is not a deciding factor.

The deciding factor is execution risk against an immovable deadline. CRANMOOR's structural advantages — owned content, managed register, no perpetual purchase — are real and worth pursuing, but they depend on a recruitment trajectory that historical performance does not support in the available window. The consequences of missing February are not merely a delay: at five months without income, drawing on a £62,000 reserve while simultaneously forfeiting £40,000 of the four-year grant, the station emerges materially weakened even if it clears the August re-sit.

ELSWICK, by contrast, passes all three Local Voice conditions on a contract, at 40 % commissioned (well under the 50 % ceiling), one hour above the speech threshold, with 34 contributors. It costs £720 more per year than the long-term CRANMOOR position, secures the transition to £96,000 a year without any reserve exposure, and leaves the board free — once Local Voice is in payment and the cap is lifted — to address the declining register and build owned programming hours without the pressure of a qualifying deadline. The register at 34 is above the 30 minimum and not an immediate crisis; the February deadline is.

---

CALL
ELSWICK

GROUNDS
ELSWICK passes all three Local Voice conditions on a signed contract with certainty, whereas CRANMOOR requires recruiting approximately fifteen new active contributors in five months — roughly four times the established rate — and the cost of missing the February assessment, a reserve draw of around £33,000 combined with £40,000 of forfeited grant income, is severe enough that the structural advantages of CRANMOOR must be pursued after the qualifying threshold is secured, not instead of securing it.
